vignette:
Linh is a 24-year-old urban planner who came to treatment after years of keeping her life narrowed to what felt manageable. She grew up in a tightly controlled home where physical abuse by a caregiver happened behind ordinary domestic routines, often in moments when she was already exposed and unable to protect herself. Some of her strongest bodily reactions now make sense against those early experiences: being looked at closely, having her body examined, or feeling suddenly nauseous can bring back the same sense of helplessness she knew as a child. What she can say clearly is not always a full picture of what happened. When she tries on purpose to remember specific incidents, her mind often seems to go blank, as if the details are sealed off. Yet the emotional force arrives anyway. She can be sitting still and suddenly feel the same fear and humiliation in her body without any image attached to it. At other times, if something does break through, what surges up most strongly is rage.

She described childhood as a period in which she learned to track other people’s movements constantly. A hand lifting too quickly, someone turning sharply toward her, a sudden shift in posture—these still register in her body before she has time to think. In sessions she said that what frightened her was how immediate it was: her shoulders tense, her attention snaps toward the movement, and the rest of the room drops away. She has come to believe that safety exists only in a very limited number of places, mostly her apartment and a few carefully chosen environments where she can control who is around her and how exposed she feels. Outside those spaces, she remains watchful, especially if people are close enough to see her closely.

That sense of exposure has followed her into adulthood in ways that are especially difficult because of how ordinary some triggers are. Medical settings are among the worst. During a recent examination, being asked to sit still while someone assessed her body made her feel abruptly detached and sick. She became nauseous in the waiting room and then more distressed when staff and other patients could see that something was wrong. Being seen in that vulnerable state felt intolerable. She did not experience it as embarrassment alone; it carried the deeper conviction that she was no longer a person with agency but something to be handled. Later she struggled to explain why the appointment had affected her so strongly, saying only that her body “went there” before she understood what was happening.

At work, Linh is thoughtful and capable, but her job in urban planning requires meetings, site visits, and sustained concentration that have become harder to manage. In conference rooms, if a colleague gestures suddenly across the table, she startles and loses the thread of discussion. On site visits she is more comfortable if she knows the layout in advance and can stay near exits or familiar corners. She often goes along with others’ preferences about schedules, assignments, or lunch plans, not because she is easygoing but because agreeing quickly feels safer than risking friction. Coworkers tend to see her as accommodating. What they do not see is the calculation beneath it: if she keeps other people comfortable, she is less likely to feel exposed or trapped.

Over the years she has also become skilled at steering away from reminders when other people bring up childhood, family, or discipline. If friends talk casually about strict parents or “crazy things that happened growing up,” she changes the subject or leaves. Afterwards she can spend hours thinking about how her life might have unfolded if none of it had happened—if she had grown up unafraid, if her body did not react the way it does, if ordinary things like a medical visit or a stranger’s sudden movement did not derail her. These thoughts do not comfort her. They sharpen her sense that what happened was profoundly unfair and that no one ever answered for it.

Underneath that anger is a harsh view of herself. She has come to see herself as weak for still reacting, weak for accommodating others, weak for not being able to simply remember and move on. At the same time, she speaks about the abuse with a flat certainty that she was treated like an object rather than a child. The combination leaves her oscillating between fury and self-contempt, often without words for either.

She sought help after a routine medical procedure ended with her crying in her car, nauseated and unable to return to work that afternoon. She was shaken by how small her world had become—how few places felt safe, how much energy it took to stay composed, how often she lost focus in meetings. What she fears most is that this is permanent, that she will always be vulnerable to being overtaken by feelings she cannot fully connect to memory. What she hopes, though she says it cautiously, is to feel like a person in her own life rather than someone bracing for the next moment of exposure.
